title: Why do triangles make structures rigid?
question: Why do triangles make structures rigid?
concept: A rectangle can shear into a parallelogram without changing its side lengths; a triangle cannot do this when its joints and members are rigid.
activity: Build a square and a triangle from drinking straws and paper fasteners. Push both sideways with equal care. Add one diagonal to the square and repeat.
evidence: Sketch each shape before and after. Record which shape changes angles.
safety: Do not climb or stand on classroom prototypes.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: Where does a bridge send its load?
question: Where does a bridge send its load?
concept: A load travels along beams, joints, supports, and foundations. Engineers call this a load path.
activity: Make two paper bridges with the same span. Change only the folded cross-section. Add coins one at a time to the same midpoint.
evidence: Record the number of coins and the first location that bends. Repeat three times and compare.
safety: Keep loads small and use only tabletop models.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: How can you draw a real-sized idea on paper?
question: How can you draw a real-sized idea on paper?
concept: Scale drawings preserve ratios. A 1:10 sketch shows each centimeter on the page as ten centimeters on the object.
activity: Measure a small table or storage box. Draw a top view at 1:10 and label the length and width.
evidence: Calculate expected drawing lengths, then measure your sketch with a ruler.
safety: Use a ruler safely; ask for help measuring large items.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: How do sensors become decisions?
question: How do sensors become decisions?
concept: A controller observes an input, compares it to a rule, and produces an output. This is an input–process–output loop.
activity: Write a rule for a rescue robot: if light is below a threshold, turn on a lamp; otherwise turn it off. Act out the rule as a team.
evidence: Make a table for five different sensor readings and your predicted outputs.
safety: Do not connect electronics to household mains voltage.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: Why does an LED need a resistor?
question: Why does an LED need a resistor?
concept: Current is limited by the resistor in a simple series LED model. Ohm’s law gives I=(Vs−Vf)/R when Vs exceeds Vf. The actual diode is not a fixed-voltage device.
activity: Use the WonderForge Circuit Lab to compare 220 Ω and 1000 Ω at the same simulated voltage. Predict the current before moving the slider.
evidence: Write down current in milliamps and estimated resistor power for both models.
safety: Simulation only. An adult must check the actual LED, supply, and resistor ratings before wiring. Never connect this example directly to a Pi GPIO pin.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: Why does an algorithm need exact instructions?
question: Why does an algorithm need exact instructions?
concept: An algorithm is an ordered, finite procedure. Computers follow instructions literally, including mistakes and missing conditions.
activity: In Robot Logic Lab, write commands to collect the energy cell before visiting the flag. Debug the first blocked move instead of rewriting everything.
evidence: Record your first command sequence, the failed step, and the smallest correction that worked.
safety: This is a virtual coding challenge; no physical robot is controlled.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: How do scientists classify rocks?
question: How do scientists classify rocks?
concept: Scientists classify minerals by evidence including hardness, streak, cleavage, and crystal structure rather than surface color alone.
activity: Sort three safe household materials by texture, luster and scratching behavior without damaging anything valuable. Research minerals later with an adult.
evidence: Create a data table with at least three observable properties per sample.
safety: Do not taste, crush or breathe dust from unknown rocks.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: What makes an experiment fair?
question: What makes an experiment fair?
concept: Changing one independent variable at a time helps reveal cause and effect. A measured response is the dependent variable.
activity: Compare how quickly the same volume of water drains through two different filter materials. Keep the container, initial volume, and height constant.
evidence: Time each test three times and write the range, not just a single result.
safety: Use clean water only. Do not drink experiment water.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: Why do crystals have repeating shapes?
question: Why do crystals have repeating shapes?
concept: An ordered microscopic arrangement may produce repeating external patterns. The final shape also depends on how a crystal grows.
activity: Build three candidate lattice patterns from equal-sized toy blocks and compare how each pattern repeats when extended.
evidence: Photograph or sketch a repeating unit and predict the next layer.
safety: Do not grow chemical crystals without adult approval.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: What must a Mars habitat provide?
question: What must a Mars habitat provide?
concept: A habitat is a system of interacting needs: air, water, temperature, radiation shielding, food, power, and waste processing. One failure can affect the others.
activity: Draw a block diagram showing how five habitat systems depend on one another. Circle the part with the most connections.
evidence: Create a failure scenario, such as power loss, and trace three consequences.
safety: Do not attempt pressure chambers or sealed human spaces.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: What changes how much power a panel can collect?
question: What changes how much power a panel can collect?
concept: For a given panel, received power changes with light intensity, area, and the angle of incoming rays. Real electrical output adds losses and efficiency.
activity: Use a flashlight and paper to compare the area of the light spot when the light hits straight on versus at an angle.
evidence: Trace each spot and estimate the area using a square grid.
safety: Never aim bright lights into anyone’s eyes. Do not stare at the Sun.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: Why do satellites keep missing Earth?
question: Why do satellites keep missing Earth?
concept: A satellite in orbit is falling under gravity while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing the surface. Real orbits are curved paths, not weightless escape from gravity.
activity: Tie a foam ball to a string and rotate it slowly in an open space with adult supervision, or sketch a ball moving with sideways velocity and gravity arrows.
evidence: Describe what changes when the sideways velocity becomes greater or smaller.
safety: Keep the activity well away from people, glass and pets.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: How does sound travel?
question: How does sound travel?
concept: Sound in air is a pressure wave. Its frequency relates to perceived pitch, while amplitude relates broadly to loudness.
activity: Tap two differently sized containers gently. Record or imitate the sounds. Try shorter and longer vibrating rubber bands on a safe box.
evidence: List the high and low pitches you hear and compare the vibrating lengths.
safety: Keep sound volumes comfortable; protect your hearing.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: How can you capture a clean sound?
question: How can you capture a clean sound?
concept: The microphone captures wanted sound plus environmental noise. Distance, room reflections, and levels change how clearly a recording communicates.
activity: Record the same short voice line from near and far away in a quiet room. Play both back at a comfortable level.
evidence: Compare clarity and background noise, then write down the setup of the clearer recording.
safety: Do not record or publish another person without their permission.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: How do repeating patterns become music?
question: How do repeating patterns become music?
concept: Rhythm organizes events in time. Repetition lets a listener predict, while variation creates surprise.
activity: Create a four-beat pattern using tabletop taps. Repeat it three times, then change the final beat. Ask your brother what changed.
evidence: Write beats as a simple grid and annotate where the variation occurs.
safety: Tap gently and avoid damaging furniture.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: What exactly does a loop do?
question: What exactly does a loop do?
concept: A loop repeats a set of operations until a count or condition changes. A loop without a useful exit can run indefinitely.
activity: Write a tiny Python for-loop to print a countdown. Then change the starting number and predict the output before running it.
evidence: Record what changes in the output and explain why the last iteration happens.
safety: Only run code you understand; do not paste unknown commands.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: How do game characters know where they are?
question: How do game characters know where they are?
concept: A 2D game commonly represents location with two coordinates, x and y. Movement updates one or both values.
activity: Draw a 7×7 grid with a robot at (0,6). Write a list of positions after each Right or Up movement.
evidence: Compare your paper trace with Robot Logic Lab and correct the first mismatch.
safety: Keep the game activities offline and share only approved creations.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.

title: What is the fastest way to find a bug?
question: What is the fastest way to find a bug?
concept: A bug is a difference between expected and observed behavior. Small, repeatable tests help locate where an assumption fails.
activity: Pick a broken sequence in Robot Logic Lab. Write your expectation for each step, execute one command at a time, and locate the first difference.
evidence: Describe the bug as: input, expected result, actual result, smallest fix.
safety: Back up files before trying unfamiliar changes.
followUp: Write one observation in Project Vault, then teach the idea to your brother.
